title: Whole Foods and Sprouts Vendor Requirements: What Natural Channel Buyers Expect
summary: Natural channel buyers like Whole Foods and Sprouts have their own strict standards. Here's what to expect before you pitch.
body_markdown:
[Tips](https://thefreshfactory.co/blog-categories/tips/)


September 16, 2026


Clean, better-for-you food and beverages are more than just a trend. In 2025, U.S. organic sales hit[$76.6 billion, growing nearly 7% year over year](https://www.supermarketperimeter.com/articles/13840-us-organic-sales-achieve-nearly-7-annual-growth-rate) (well ahead of conventional grocery). Natural grocery store chains like Whole Foods and Sprouts are paying attention. Sprouts alone surpassed[450 stores in 2025](https://www.modernretail.co/operations/sprouts-hopes-to-grow-from-450-stores-to-about-1400/) , and CEO Jack Sinclair has said Sprouts hopes to eventually reach 1,400 stores nationwide


There’s a big opportunity for better-for-you brands to take advantage of the clean label craze, but breaking into the natural channel requires clearing a specific set of standards, and they look different than what[mass retailers](https://thefreshfactory.co/blog/getting-into-walmart-target/) ask for. Read on for the requirements of two of the biggest players in the natural CPG retail space: Whole Foods and Sprouts.


## The Natural Channel Plays by Its Own Rules


While national chain groceries like Walmart tend to look for mainstream appeal, natural retailers are built around ingredient philosophy first. Whole Foods and Sprouts will take a chance on something new as long as it’s clean, natural, and better-for-you. But the tradeoff is that “natural” and “clean label” aren’t just marketing language. Each retailer backs those words with a specific, documented standard that must be met.


## Whole Foods Vendor Requirements


### Certifications & Audits


Like most retailers, Whole Foods requires annual third-party audits. They accept either a GFSI-recognized standard — SQF, BRCGS, PrimusGFS, or FSSC 22000 — or a non-GFSI audit like GMP certification, depending on the type of supplier. A SQF-certified facility like those at The Fresh Factory satisfies this requirement.


### Ingredient Standards


Whole Foods has strict quality standards. They maintain a[published list of more than 300 prohibited ingredients](https://www.wholefoodsmarket.com/quality-standards/food-ingredient-standards) , including hydrogenated fats, artificial sweeteners, and several synthetic dyes and preservatives. Vendors are responsible for checking that list at least quarterly to confirm ongoing compliance.


### EDI Requirements


Like most retailers, Whole Foods requires EDI capability for purchase orders, invoices, acknowledgements, and ASNs. You can learn more by signing up for their[Supplier Portal](https://grocerycentral.amazon.com/) .


### Buying Structure


Whole Foods buys products at three levels: locally, regionally, and nationally. Often the easiest way to get a food in the door is to start locally and prove your product can perform. It’s also important to note that getting accepted in one region doesn’t mean placement anywhere else. Distribution isn’t all-or-nothing.


### Where to Start


The first step to getting into Whole Foods is ensuring you meet their rigorous quality standards, both for your product and its packaging. From there, sign up for the Whole Foods[Supplier Portal](https://grocerycentral.amazon.com/) . (For additional discoverability if you haven’t already connected with a buyer or local “forager,” you can also create a RangeMe profile to help draw attention to your product.)


To learn more about becoming a Whole Foods supplier, and to learn about the Local and Emerging Accelerator Program (LEAP) program, visit[here](https://www.wholefoodsmarket.com/company-info/information-potential-suppliers) .


## Sprouts Vendor Requirements


### Certifications & Audits


Sprouts requires third-party food safety and quality certification and a documented recall process before a vendor is onboarded, along with a risk assessment covering the product category, the vendor, and the brand itself.


### Ingredient Standards


Sprouts also prohibits certain ingredients, with a proprietary vetting process specific to each category.[New product submissions](https://about.sprouts.com/new-item-submission-process/) must include an ingredient statement, a nutritional facts panel (per the new 2020 standards), and an allergen statement.


### EDI Requirements


Sprouts vendors need EDI capability to receive purchase orders and submit acknowledgements, invoices, and ASNs.


### Required Submission Details


Sprouts publishes a list of information you should have before you submit a product. You should check the most[up-to-date information](https://about.sprouts.com/things-to-know/) on sprouts.com for the latest details, but this list is accurate as of September 2026:


- Vendor Name
- Vendor Contact Information


- First Name, Last Name, Phone Number, Email Address


- Broker Contact Information


- First Name, Last Name, Phone Number, Email Address


- Item Details


- UPC or PLU (depending on type of item), Item # (if you have it), Brand, Product Description


- Individual Size Specifications


- Height, Width and Depth


- Sell Size Specifications


- Case Pack, Case Weight (Produce Only), Individual Size, UOM


- Shipping (per Case) Information


- Gross Weight, Net Weight, Case Length, Case Width, Case Height


- Pallet Configuration


- Pallet TI & HI, Total Cases per pallet


- Warehouse Information


- Temperature Range, COO, Seasonality


- Cost Information


- MSRP, Regular Wholesale Cost, F.O.B. Cost, Delivered Cost


- Other Information


- Ongoing Discount% ; EDLP%


- Certifications


- Organic, Non-GMO, Gluten-free, etc.


### Submission Schedule


Sprouts publishes their “[Category Review Calendar](https://about.sprouts.com/full-reset-calendar/) ,” which outlines submission dates for specific product categories based on when the retailer plans to accept new products.


It’s also helpful to know that Sprouts brings a significant team to[Natural Products Expo West](https://thefreshfactory.co/blog/trends-expo-west-2026/) every March and names it directly as a place to meet buyers and introduce new products, which gives brands a concrete, scheduled opportunity for face time.


### Where to Start


You can read more about Sprouts vendor policies, including free fill and merchandising fees,[here](https://about.sprouts.com/vendor-policies-2/) .


## Other Natural Retailers Worth Knowing


Whole Foods and Sprouts get most of the attention, but they’re not the only doors into this channel. A few worth having on the radar:


- **Natural Grocers** sources primarily through RangeMe or direct email submission, requires a $1 million insurance rider, and reviews new items on a monthly cycle. Produce submissions need a current USDA Organic Certificate on file, and mockups aren’t accepted — Natural Grocers wants full production samples with registered UPCs.
- **Fresh Thyme Market** is actively rebuilding its own-brand and assortment strategy and has said publicly it’s looking for new supplier partners as part of that push. Vendors can submit through RangeMe or reach out directly to the category manager for their product with a sell sheet, UPCs, SRPs, and case pack details.
- **The Fresh Market** also sources through RangeMe, with a published Supplier Code of Conduct and standard food safety/permit documentation expected of every vendor.


None of these carry the volume of Whole Foods or Sprouts, but for a brand building regional natural-channel presence, they’re documented paths worth working in parallel.


## How a Co-Manufacturer Reduces the Operational Risk


The natural channel’s requirements map closely to what a clean-label co-manufacturer already has built into daily operations. SQF certification satisfies the GFSI standard both Whole Foods and Sprouts recognize. Production experience built around clean-label formulation is a direct answer to Whole Foods’ ingredient standards, not a retrofit. And audit-ready documentation is table stakes for a facility that’s already producing to this standard for other customers.


Getting a natural retailer to say yes still comes down to the product and the[pitch](https://thefreshfactory.co/blog/pitching-food-brand/) . Having a manufacturing partner who already operates inside these standards just means there’s one less thing to figure out under deadline.
